The AI Brief
An overview of the UK’s 
Artificial Intelligence sector

This report analyses the ambitious private companies operating in the UK’s artificial 
intelligence sector and the supporting mechanisms for growth. With almost 700 active 
ambitious companies, and a healthy supply of capital from investors across the 
ecosystem, AI is becoming an ever increasing strength of the UK high-growth economy.
Artificial Intelligence, or AI, encompasses a range of computer programmes intended to 
solve problems requiring learning, understanding context or otherwise operating with 
autonomy from humans using human-like thought processes and the processing power 
of computers.

As we’ll see in this overview of the sector, AI has been around for a while, but has only 
really taken oﬀ within the last five years. Technology has developed drastically in this 
time, and with huge investor appetite the private market is truly flourishing. As 
discussion increasingly turn towards the dangers and responsibilities that come with 
powerful AI technology, governments are also supporting and preparing to shape growth 
in the industry. 
There are a couple of reasons for this; to stay ahead of the international competition, in 
terms of both national security and establishing the country as a global thought leader 
to attract further investment; and to form appropriate legislation that protects citizens, 
whilst nurturing an environment conducive to innovation. As of yet, regulations remain 
lax, allowing innovators to explore the full range of opportunities that ambitious AI 
companies can oﬀer.

We use 8 criteria to identify high-growth 
and ambitious companies. Each of these is 
a sign of external validation that a business 
is either actively growing or creating 
ambitious growth plans. 
All companies featured in this report have 
met at least one of these growth triggers.
What do we mean by “ambitious”?
Equity investment
Accelerator attendance
Scaleups
MBO/MBI
Venture debt
Grant recipients
High-growth lists
Academic spinouts

There are 697 active, ambitious AI companies 
in the UK.
An additional 28 have exited the market, either 
through an IPO or an acquisition, and 92 are 
no longer trading.  
With over 50% of AI companies in the seed 
stage, and few reaching the later stages of 
growth at this point, it’s clear that the sector is 
nascent. Each of these companies has the 
potential to transform society with their 
proprietary tech, but most will need to use 
external support to reach commercialisation. 
Stages of evolution

Indeed, the sector has seen a sudden surge in 
popularity over the past few years, with 130 
high-growth AI companies having been 
incorporated in 2015 alone. 
The decline in number since then is simply a 
time lag; companies incorporated in the last 
three years have not had as much time to gain 
traction and exhibit high-growth. 
The race is on for investors to pick out the 
most promising early stage ventures from the 
rapidly growing crowd.

AI is an IP driven sector; 9% of high-growth AI 
companies have spun out of an academic institution, 
and 30% have received innovation grants. These 
figures are significantly higher than the sector 
agnostic average of 3% and 17% respectively. 
These companies are backed by notable amounts of 
equity, with 76% raising investment since 2011, 
compared to just 53% across all sectors. 
At 39%, AI also has a high rate of accelerator 
attendances (compared to 22% across all 
high-growth companies).

Methods of growth

While London dominates the UK’s AI scene with 
505 companies (62%) headquartered in the 
capital, there are also substantial hubs around 
Cambridge (28), Edinburgh (17) and Oxford (15).
It’s no coincidence that these cities all host 
world class universities. 12 of the of AI startups 
in Oxford (80%) have been spun out from 
academic institutions. There are only five in 
Cambridge, but a further six companies have 
spunout from the University of Cambridge and 
chosen headquarters in other cities, including 
leading AI unicorn, Darktrace. 
Geographical distribution
GEOGRAPHICAL 
DISTRIBUTION 
OF COMPANIES

AI companies have secured consistently 
increasing amounts of equity investment since 
2011. It is one of the few sectors to have raised 
more money in 2018 than 2017 and secure a 
higher volume of deals. 
Using Q1 2019 investment figures as a 
reference, we expect funding levels to surpass 
the £1b mark for the first time. With just 87 
deals completed in the first quarter of this 
year, the number of deals completed by the 
end of the year is less likely to match the 
record level in 2018. 
Fundraising statistics
NUMBER OF DEALS AND AMOUNT RAISED

The number of deals secured by seed-stage 
companies was down across all sectors in 2018 – 
even in fintech. But AI managed to buck this trend, 
securing 13% more seed stage deals in 2018 than 
in 2017. 
This is incredibly reassuring to see amidst such 
economic uncertainty, and shows there is 
substantial support for ambitious AI companies 
choosing to grow in the UK. Seed funding is 
especially important for a sector with such a focus 
on research and development, helping companies 
to survive beyond this capital intensive phase. 
Fundraising statistics
NUMBER OF DEALS BY STAGE OF EVOLUTION

In an eﬀort to establish the UK as a global 
leader in AI, the government is seeking ways to 
nurture ambitious companies in the sector. 
These plans were set out in the Industrial 
Strategy, published in 2017. 
Reflecting these intentions is the growing 
number of grants allocated to AI companies by 
government bodies such as Innovate UK. 
Considering the majority of grants tend to be 
allocated later in the year, 2019 is on track to 
see more grants allocated than ever before, in 
terms of both number and value. 
Grant statistics
NUMBER OF GRANTS AND AMOUNT ALLOCATED

Top investors
Parkwalk Advisors are the most prolific investors 
into UK AI since 2011, with 19 deals across 8 
companies. Their portfolio includes University of 
Oxford spinout Oxbotica, insurtech platform 
Cytora, and adtech company Mirriad, which IPO’d 
on the AIM for £25.4m in December 2017. 
Meanwhile, Amadeus Capital Partners have the 
highest number of AI companies in their 
portfolio, with 17 announced funding rounds 
across 11 companies, including phishing 
software Tessian and unicorn startup Graphcore.
